            Plaintiff Andrea Hull alleges as follows:
22
                                             INTRODUCTION
23
            1.      Since 1872, California law has guaranteed every person the right to pursue any
24
     lawful profession, trade, or business. Business and Professions Code section 16600 provides that,
25
     except as otherwise permitted by statute, “every contract by which anyone is restrained from
26
     engaging in a lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void.” The
27
     California Supreme Court has confirmed that this prohibition is absolute in the employment
28


                                                 COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702         Document 1        Filed 07/24/26      Page 2 of 27



 1   context: there is no “narrow restraint” exception, and covenants not to compete and covenants not

 2   to solicit customers are void no matter how reasonable an employer believes them to be. Edwards

 3   v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937.

 4          2.      In 2023, the Legislature reinforced this policy. Senate Bill 699 added Business and

 5   Professions Code section 16600.5, which provides that any contract void under section 16600 is

 6   unenforceable “regardless of where and when the contract was signed,” forbids an employer or

 7   former employer from attempting to enforce such a contract “regardless of whether the contract

 8   was signed and the employment was maintained outside of California,” declares that an employer

 9   who enters into or attempts to enforce such a contract “commits a civil violation,” and gives

10   employees, former employees, and prospective employees a private right of action for injunctive

11   relief and actual damages, with mandatory attorneys’ fees and costs to a prevailing employee.

12   Assembly Bill 1076 added section 16600.1, which makes it unlawful to include a noncompete

13   clause in an employment contract or to require an employee to enter a noncompete agreement,

14   and required employers to notify current and former California employees in individualized

15   writings that any such clauses in their agreements are void. AB 1076 also amended section 16600

16   itself to provide that the statute reaches restraints “no matter how narrowly tailored” (§ 16600,

17   subd. (b)(1)) and that it is “not limited to contracts where the person being restrained is a party to

18   the contract” (§ 16600, subd. (b)(2)).

19          3.      Defendant Epic Systems Corporation (“Epic”) is the dominant vendor of electronic

20   health record (“EHR”) software in the United States. Epic, directly and through its wholly owned

21   staffing subsidiary, Defendant Boost, Inc. (“Boost”), requires its California-based employees to

22   sign a Wisconsin-law form agreement containing a one-year covenant not to compete that bars

23   former employees from working for any “Direct Competitor” on an Epic-controlled list

24   (including Amazon, Apple, Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle Health, and Salesforce); from

25   establishing or aiding any new business that overlaps with Epic’s products; from soliciting Epic

26   customers or prospects for competitive purposes; from being employed by any Epic customer or

27   prospective customer in any role that involves Epic software; and from working for Epic’s

28   consultants and “Cooperative Partners” in overlapping healthcare software or services work.

                                                      -2-
                                                  COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702         Document 1        Filed 07/24/26      Page 3 of 27



 1   Because Epic’s customers include most significant health systems in the United States, the

 2   covenant operates to exclude former Epic employees from virtually the entire health-information-

 3   technology industry in which they built their careers.

 4           4.     Epic backstops these void covenants with restraints at the other end of the labor

 5   market: provisions in its customer and partner contracts — including, on information and belief,

 6   no-hire, no-poach, and 12-month “cooling off” provisions — that restrict Epic’s customers from

 7   hiring or using former Epic employees no matter what the employees’ own agreements say.

 8   Epic’s human resources department put it plainly, in writing: “customer contracts often include

 9   provisions related to hiring, which would still apply to those organizations.” And Epic polices the

10   gate itself: it controls the “UserWeb” credentials, certifications, training, and conference access

11   that anyone working with Epic’s platforms needs, and it denies those credentials to recent former

12   employees — while offering them to virtually everyone else — as a means of enforcing its

13   restraints.

14           5.     Epic does not treat its competition restraints as dead letters. It enforces them —

15   selectively, and as an instrument of loyalty. Epic maintains a waiver program under which it will

16   excuse its noncompete for a departing employee who has served at least seven years at Epic and

17   three years at Boost and who remains for a year at the Epic customer seeking to hire them. The

18   restraints, in other words, are not calibrated to protect trade secrets; they are calibrated to keep

19   employees and customers in the fold.

20           6.     Plaintiff Andrea Hull is a California resident, living in Concord in the San

21   Francisco Bay Area, who devoted approximately eleven and a half years of her career to the Epic

22   Group, most recently working remotely from Concord for Boost. In March 2026, she left Boost

23   and joined Abbott Diabetes Care (“Abbott”) as an EHR Implementation Manager — a customer-

24   side role developing the strategy to scale Abbott’s continuous glucose monitoring (“CGM”)

25   device integration with Epic’s platforms, including “Epic Aura,” across more than 400 health

26   systems. The role advances the adoption of Epic’s own products. Abbott’s legal department

27   vetted the hire before extending the offer.

28

                                                      -3-
                                                   COMPLAINT
         Case 3:26-cv-07702           Document 1       Filed 07/24/26      Page 4 of 27



 1          7.         Within weeks, Epic denied Ms. Hull the UserWeb credentials her job at Abbott

 2   requires — credentials needed for conference registration and for access to Epic technical

 3   documentation — citing a one-year “cooling off” period, and made its position clear to Abbott: as

 4   an Abbott program manager relayed it in writing, “we were informed former Epic employees

 5   should not be working on Epic direct, related work for 12 months.” Abbott — dependent on its

 6   commercial relationship with Epic — reacted exactly as Epic intended. It removed Ms. Hull from

 7   scheduled customer trips, pulled her from Epic’s XGM conference, directed her not to engage

 8   with Epic-affiliated health systems at Becker’s, an industry conference she was actively

 9   supporting, and excluded her from certain internal and external meetings. Career advancement

10   opportunities outlined in her first weeks have been delayed or lost. Those restrictions remain in

11   place today.

12          8.         When Ms. Hull asked Epic’s human resources department whether an updated

13   employee agreement existed that complied with California law, Epic confirmed in writing that no

14   updated agreement exists and that the agreement she signed remains the applicable one — and

15   pointed to the hiring restrictions in Epic’s customer contracts. Each of the restraints described

16   above — the covenant not to compete, the customer and employee nonsolicitation provisions, the

17   de facto restraints embedded in Epic’s perpetual confidentiality and return-of-property provisions,

18   the Wisconsin choice-of-law and forum provisions, the no-hire, no-poach, and “cooling off”

19   provisions in Epic’s customer and partner contracts, and the credential denials used to enforce

20   them — is void or unlawful under California law, including Business and Professions Code

21   sections 16600, 16600.1, and 16600.5, the Unfair Competition Law, and the common law right to

22   fair procedure.

23          9.         The complaint seeks declaratory and injunctive relief, including public injunctive

24   relief, consistent with California’s unfair competition law. She asks the Court to declare these

25   provisions void, to enjoin Defendants from enforcing or attempting to enforce them — against her

26   and against every other California-resident former employee of the Epic Group — and to award

27   her reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs as provided by statute. She does not seek damages in this

28

                                                       -4-
                                                   COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702           Document 1     Filed 07/24/26      Page 5 of 27



 1   action. The object of this Complaint is not compensation; it is the freedom of California workers

 2   to practice their professions.

 3                                                 PARTIES

 4          10.     Plaintiff Andrea Hull is an individual who resides and is domiciled in Concord,

 5   Contra Costa County, California, and at all relevant times has primarily resided and worked in

 6   California. Ms. Hull is a former employee of Epic and Boost. She is currently employed by

 7   Abbott as an EHR Implementation Manager with Abbott Diabetes Care, based in Alameda,

 8   California.

 9          11.     Defendant Epic Systems Corporation is a corporation organized under the laws of

10   Wisconsin with its principal place of business in Verona, Wisconsin, and is therefore a citizen of

11   Wisconsin. Epic develops, markets, licenses, and supports EHR software and related

12   implementation services used by health systems throughout the United States, including

13   throughout California. Epic transacts substantial business in California, licenses its software to

14   numerous California health systems, and employs California residents, including remote

15   employees who reside and work in California.

16          12.     Defendant Boost, Inc. is, on information and belief, a corporation organized under

17   the laws of Wisconsin with its principal place of business in Verona, Wisconsin, and is therefore

18   a citizen of Wisconsin. Boost is a wholly owned subsidiary of Epic. Boost is in the business, as a

19   subcontractor to Epic or other companies in the “Epic Group,” of providing staff to fill

20   implementation-team roles — typically on the customer side — and to take on special projects

21   related to customers’ use of Epic software. Boost employs remote employees who reside and

22   work in California.

23          13.     At all relevant times, Epic and Boost operated as an integrated enterprise and/or as

24   joint employers of Ms. Hull and other California-based employees. Among other things: Boost is

25   wholly owned by Epic; the Boost employment agreement is written for the benefit of the entire

26   “Epic Group” and names Epic as an intended third-party beneficiary entitled to enforce it; Epic’s

27   policies and procedures manual (the “Redbook”) governs Boost employees; exceptions to the

28   covenant not to compete may be granted only by “an Epic HR director”; Boost employees sign a

                                                     -5-
                                                 COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702         Document 1        Filed 07/24/26       Page 6 of 27



 1   Mutual Arbitration Agreement directly with “Epic Systems Corporation, together with its related

 2   and affiliated companies”; and Epic’s human resources department administers and enforces the

 3   Boost agreement, as it did with respect to Ms. Hull. Epic and Boost are referred to collectively as

 4   “Epic” or “Defendants” except where the distinction matters.

 5          14.     The true names and capacities of Defendants sued as Does 1 through 10 are

 6   unknown to Ms. Hull, who will amend this Complaint to allege their true names and capacities

 7   when ascertained. On information and belief, each Doe defendant is an affiliate, subsidiary, agent,

 8   or co-conspirator of Epic or Boost, is responsible in some manner for the conduct alleged herein,

 9   and no Doe defendant is a citizen of California.

10          15.     At all relevant times, each Defendant acted as the agent, alter ego, joint venturer,

11   co-conspirator, and/or aider and abettor of each other Defendant, and acted within the course and

12   scope of that relationship with the knowledge, consent, approval, and ratification of each other

13   Defendant.

14                                     JURISDICTION AND VENUE

15          16.     This Court has subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1332(a)(1). Ms. Hull

16   is a citizen of California; Epic and Boost are citizens of Wisconsin; and complete diversity exists.

17   The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs. In an action for

18   injunctive and declaratory relief, the amount in controversy is measured by the value of the object

19   of the litigation. The object of this litigation is Ms. Hull’s right to perform her profession free of

20   Defendants’ restraints — during the restraint period and beyond — and the value of that right, to

21   either party, plainly exceeds the jurisdictional threshold, as do the mandatory statutory attorneys’

22   fees recoverable under Business and Professions Code section 16600.5, subdivision (e)(2).

23          17.     This Court has personal jurisdiction over Defendants. Defendants transact

24   substantial business in California; employed Ms. Hull, knowing that she resided and worked in

25   California; directed the enforcement conduct alleged herein at a California resident and her

26   California employer; and have purposefully availed themselves of the benefits of the California

27   market, including by licensing software and selling implementation services to California health

28   systems.

                                                      -6-
                                                  COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702         Document 1       Filed 07/24/26      Page 7 of 27



 1          18.     Venue is proper in this District under 28 U.S.C. § 1391(b)(2) because a substantial

 2   part of the events giving rise to the claims occurred in this District: Ms. Hull resides in Contra

 3   Costa County, within this District, and worked for Defendants remotely from her home in this

 4   District; her employer is based in Alameda County; and Defendants directed their enforcement

 5   conduct into this District.

 6          19.     Intradistrict Assignment. Assignment to the San Francisco or Oakland Division

 7   is proper under Civil Local Rule 3-2(c) and (d) because a substantial part of the events giving rise

 8   to the claims occurred in the Counties of Contra Costa and Alameda, from which civil actions are

 9   assigned to the San Francisco Division or the Oakland Division.

10          20.     The Wisconsin choice-of-law and forum provisions in Ms. Hull’s form

11   employment agreement do not affect jurisdiction, venue, or governing law. Under Business and

12   Professions Code section 16600.5, subdivisions (a) and (b), the void restraints are unenforceable,

13   and may not be the subject of enforcement attempts, regardless of where and when the contract

14   was signed. In addition, the agreement was presented to Ms. Hull as a standard-form condition of

15   employment after January 1, 2017, and she was not individually represented by counsel in

16   negotiating its terms; under Labor Code section 925, any provision requiring adjudication outside

17   California or depriving her of the substantive protection of California law is voidable by her, and

18   Ms. Hull hereby voids those provisions. Under Labor Code section 925(b), this controversy is to

19   be adjudicated in California under California law.

20                                      FACTUAL ALLEGATIONS

21        A.      California’s Settled Public Policy Against Restraints on Employee Mobility

22          21.     Business and Professions Code section 16600, subdivision (a), provides: “Except

23   as provided in this chapter, every contract by which anyone is restrained from engaging in a

24   lawful profession, trade, or business of any kind is to that extent void.” Subdivision (b)(1), added

25   by Assembly Bill 1076 effective January 1, 2024, directs that the section “shall be read broadly,

26   in accordance with Edwards v. Arthur Andersen LLP (2008) 44 Cal.4th 937, to void the

27   application of any noncompete agreement in an employment context, or any noncompete clause

28   in an employment contract, no matter how narrowly tailored, that does not satisfy an exception in

                                                      -7-
                                                 COMPLAINT
          Case 3:26-cv-07702        Document 1        Filed 07/24/26      Page 8 of 27



 1   this chapter.” Subdivision (b)(2) provides that the section “shall not be limited to contracts where

 2   the person being restrained is a party to the contract.” None of the statutory exceptions — which

 3   concern the sale or dissolution of businesses and ownership interests — applies here.

 4            22.   Business and Professions Code section 16600.1, subdivision (a), makes it

 5   “unlawful to include a noncompete clause in an employment contract, or to require an employee

 6   to enter a noncompete agreement, that does not satisfy an exception in this chapter.” Subdivision

 7   (b) required employers, by February 14, 2024, to provide individualized written notice to current

 8   employees, and to former employees employed after January 1, 2022, whose contracts include a

 9   noncompete clause, that the noncompete clause is void. Subdivision (c) provides that a violation

10   of section 16600.1 “constitutes an act of unfair competition” under the Unfair Competition Law,

11   Business and Professions Code section 17200 et seq.

12            23.   Business and Professions Code section 16600.5 provides that any contract that is

13   void under the chapter “is unenforceable regardless of where and when the contract was signed”

14   (subd. (a)); that an employer or former employer “shall not attempt to enforce a contract that is

15   void under this chapter regardless of whether the contract was signed and the employment was

16   maintained outside of California” (subd. (b)); that an employer “shall not enter into a contract

17   with an employee or prospective employee that includes a provision that is void under this

18   chapter” (subd. (c)); and that an employer that enters into such a contract or attempts to enforce it

19   “commits a civil violation” (subd. (d)). Subdivision (e) authorizes an employee, former employee,

20   or prospective employee to bring a private action for injunctive relief or the recovery of actual

21   damages, or both, and entitles a prevailing employee to recover reasonable attorneys’ fees and

22   costs.

23            24.   California courts have long applied these protections to California employees

24   notwithstanding out-of-state employers and out-of-state choice-of-law provisions. (Application

25   Group, Inc. v. Hunter Group, Inc. (1998) 61 Cal.App.4th 881.) California courts have likewise

26   held that contractual provisions that nominally protect “confidential information” but in operation

27   prevent a former employee from using the general skills, knowledge, and acquaintances acquired

28   during employment function as void restraints of trade. (Dowell v. Biosense Webster, Inc. (2009)

                                                     -8-
                                                 COMPLAINT
         Case 3:26-cv-07702          Document 1      Filed 07/24/26      Page 9 of 27



 1   179 Cal.App.4th 564; AMN Healthcare, Inc. v. Aya Healthcare Services, Inc. (2018) 28

 2   Cal.App.5th 923.) And California courts refuse to enforce no-hire provisions in contracts between

 3   companies where, as applied, they restrain employee mobility. (VL Systems, Inc. v. Unisen, Inc.

 4   (2007) 152 Cal.App.4th 708.)

 5                           B.     Epic, Boost, and Ms. Hull’s Employment

 6          25.     Epic is the largest EHR vendor in the United States. Its software manages the

 7   medical records of a majority of Americans, and its customers include most large health systems

 8   in the country, including throughout California. Companies across the health-care economy —

 9   medical-device manufacturers, digital-health companies, payers, and consultancies — must work

10   with and around Epic’s platforms, and they hire experienced Epic-trained professionals to do so.

11          26.     Boost is Epic’s remote-staffing arm. Boost employees work remotely from

12   anywhere in the contiguous United States, are staffed onto Epic customer projects, and perform

13   customer-side implementation work — system build, testing, training, and project and program

14   management — under the Epic umbrella.

15          27.     Ms. Hull devoted approximately eleven and a half years of her career to the Epic

16   Group, rising through positions of increasing trust across three countries. She joined Epic in

17   Madison, Wisconsin in 2014, shortly after earning her law degree from the University of

18   Wisconsin. As a Project Manager (Madison, 2014–2016), she led enterprise testing for multi-

19   hospital EHR implementations. As an Implementation Director (Madison, 2016–2018), she

20   delivered add-on EHR implementation projects. As a Boost Consultant (Denver, 2018–2020), she

21   co-designed the enterprise training and operational-readiness program for an implementation

22   serving more than 200,000 users across multiple states. As Contract Manager (Trondheim,

23   Norway, 2020–2022), she managed implementation and development compliance for a first-in-

24   country contract and provided strategy support to Legal, Development, and Implementation

25   leadership in negotiations. And as the first international public policy team member (Bristol,

26   England, 2022–2025), she represented Epic itself before government stakeholders and trade

27   associations in multiple jurisdictions, and co-founded a global policy council with Epic customer

28   representatives from 13 countries.

                                                     -9-
                                                COMPLAINT
         Case 3:26-cv-07702         Document 1        Filed 07/24/26       Page 10 of 27



 1          28.     Returning to the United States as a Boost Consultant working from Concord,

 2   California, Ms. Hull designed enterprise transformation and change-management programs for

 3   healthcare organizations spanning more than 80 sites. Everything in that career — the

 4   certifications, the product fluency, the customer relationships, the implementation methods — is

 5   professional skill, knowledge, and experience built over more than a decade within the Epic

 6   Group. It is precisely the general human capital that California law guarantees a former employee

 7   the right to carry into her next position. And it is the professional foundation that Defendants’

 8   covenants, customer-contract restraints, and credential denials now render largely unusable in the

 8   enforce contracts that are void under the chapter, in violation of Business and Professions Code

 9   section 16600.5, subdivision (b), and have committed civil violations under subdivision (d).

10           73.    Ms. Hull is entitled to a declaration that these provisions are void and

11   unenforceable as applied to her and to California-resident former employees of Defendants; to

12   preliminary and permanent injunctive relief barring Defendants from maintaining, invoking,

13   applying, or enforcing them as to her and as to California-resident former employees; and to her

14   reasonable attorneys’ fees and costs under section 16600.5, subdivision (e)(2).

15                                    THIRD CLAIM FOR RELIEF

16                       Unfair Competition (Bus. & Prof. Code § 17200 et seq.)

17                                        (Against All Defendants)

18           74.    Ms. Hull incorporates each of the foregoing paragraphs as though fully set forth

19   here.

20           75.    Defendants’ conduct constitutes unlawful business acts and practices within the

21   meaning of Business and Professions Code section 17200, including: entering into and

22   maintaining contracts containing provisions void under section 16600; including noncompete

23   clauses in employment contracts and requiring employees to enter noncompete agreements in

24   violation of section 16600.1, subdivision (a); failing to provide the individualized written notices

25   required by section 16600.1, subdivision (b) — a violation that constitutes an act of unfair

26   competition by operation of section 16600.1, subdivision (c); attempting to enforce void contracts

27   in violation of section 16600.5; maintaining, invoking, and applying no-hire, no-poach, and

28   “cooling off” provisions void under section 16600, subdivision (b)(2); requiring employees, as a

 1   condition of employment, to agree in writing to terms Defendants know to be prohibited by law,

 2   in violation of Labor Code section 432.5; and excluding Ms. Hull from occupationally necessary

 3   credentials in violation of the common law right to fair procedure, as alleged in paragraphs 76 and

 4   77.

 5          76.       Under California common law, a private entity that controls access to a resource or

 6   affiliation practically necessary to the pursuit of an occupation may not exclude a person from it

 7   arbitrarily, or for reasons contrary to public policy, and must afford fair procedure. (Potvin v.

 8   Metropolitan Life Ins. Co. (2000) 22 Cal.4th 1060; Ezekial v. Winkley (1977) 20 Cal.3d 267.)

 9   Epic controls such a resource. Individual UserWeb credentials — and the conference registration,

10   technical documentation, and certification maintenance they gate — are practically necessary to

11   pursue the occupation of an Epic-certified health-information-technology professional, an

12   occupation practiced across thousands of employers. Epic is the sole source of these credentials

13   and holds them out to the public of certified professionals, including persons unaffiliated with any

14   Epic customer.

15          77.       Epic excluded Ms. Hull from this resource arbitrarily and for reasons contrary to

16   the fundamental public policy of California: it denied her application pursuant to an unwritten

17   “cooling off” policy that appears in no published terms, in order to enforce restraints that

18   California law declares void, without disclosed criteria, without a meaningful opportunity to be

19   heard, and while granting access to similarly situated certified professionals — indeed, while

20   maintaining a discretionary waiver program that excuses the same restraints for employees and

21   customers who demonstrate sufficient loyalty to Epic. Epic’s violation of the common law right

22   to fair procedure is an unlawful business practice under section 17200.

23          78.       Defendants’ conduct is also unfair within the meaning of section 17200. Under

24   Cel-Tech Communications, Inc. v. Los Angeles Cellular Telephone Co. (1999) 20 Cal.4th 163,

25   conduct is unfair where it threatens an incipient violation of an antitrust law, or violates the policy

26   or spirit of those laws, or otherwise significantly threatens or harms competition. Defendants’

27   denial of UserWeb credentials and conference access to recent former employees — implemented

28   to enforce void restraints and coordinated with the hiring restrictions in Defendants’ customer

 1   contracts — violates the policy and spirit of Business and Professions Code sections 16600 and

 2   16720 and significantly harms competition in the labor market for Epic-skilled professionals,

 3   even to the extent any individual denial is recast as unilateral conduct. Defendants’ conduct

 4   further offends the established public policies of this State embodied in sections 16600 through

 5   16600.5, and its gravity — the exclusion of California workers from their professions — vastly

 6   outweighs any utility, of which there is none.

 7            79.    Ms. Hull has suffered injury in fact and lost money or property as a result of

 8   Defendants’ unfair competition, including lost compensation, benefits, and professional

 9   opportunities — among them the Epic IT leadership positions at California health systems that

10   she was deterred from pursuing, as alleged in paragraphs 40 and 41. She nonetheless seeks no

11   restitution and no damages in this action; she seeks only injunctive and declaratory relief, and her

12   attorneys’ fees and costs as permitted by law.

13            80.    Ms. Hull seeks injunctive relief under section 17203, including orders: enjoining

14   Defendants from enforcing or attempting to enforce the void provisions against Ms. Hull or any

15   other California-resident employee or former employee; requiring Defendants to withdraw, in

16   writing, their statements to Abbott regarding restrictions on Ms. Hull’s work; enjoining

17   Defendants from denying Ms. Hull UserWeb credentials, conference access, or certification

18   maintenance on the basis of her former employment or any “cooling off” period; enjoining

19   Defendants from maintaining, invoking, or applying customer-contract no-hire, no-poach, or

20   “cooling off” provisions as to California-resident former employees; and requiring Defendants to

21   provide the written notices mandated by section 16600.1, subdivision (b). The injunctive relief

22   sought is, in substantial part, public injunctive relief: it would prohibit acts that threaten future

23   injury to the general public of California workers, and its primary beneficiaries are the California-

24   resident employees and former employees of the Epic Group at large, not Ms. Hull alone. (McGill

25   v. Citibank, N.A. (2017) 2 Cal.5th 945.)
